summary: Profile of New York photographer Tyler Mitchell, who at 23 became the first black photographer to shoot an American Vogue cover (Beyoncé) and later shot the controversial Kamala Harris Vogue cover. Three of his works appear in the NGV Triennial, where his lightly staged scenes of black American leisure aim to build a new visual narrative. He discusses challenging 'visual regimes', his path from film student to photographer, and his relaxed view of career ups and downs.
one_line: Photographer Tyler Mitchell, famed for his Beyoncé and Kamala Harris Vogue covers, shows idyllic black American leisure scenes at the NGV Triennial.
key_facts: Tyler Mitchell was 23 when he became the first black photographer to shoot the cover of American Vogue; his subject was Beyoncé.
Mitchell has more than 500,00 Instagram followers, according to the article, and has exhibited around the world in the five years since the Beyoncé cover.
His portrait of Kamala Harris in sneakers and casual clothing was used for the Vogue cover of February 2021 and prompted swift social media backlash.
Critics asked why his alternative, more formal image of Harris was not used; Vogue later issued a limited edition using the more formal shot.
Three of Mitchell's works are in the NGV's Triennial exhibition, whose theme is 'Magic, Matter, Memory': Picnic, Albany, Georgia, and Vastness.
Mitchell describes his approach as 'lightly staged moments', setting up scenarios where families enjoy real leisure in outdoor spaces such as open pastures and fields.
He says his work is 'A consideration of joy, perseverance and self-determination against the backdrop of history.'
Mitchell wants to challenge 'visual regimes', and sees photojournalism as a well from which people construct ideas of how others live.
A Glint of Possibility, one of his favourite works, shows a teenage boy on a tyre swing over a river studying his own reflection.
As a 20-year-old film student at New York University, Mitchell took a documentary photography course in Havana, Cuba, and became drawn to still photography's accessibility.
He has said he has never been to Australia and finds it exciting to have a new conversation on a new continent with his work.
Mitchell published one monograph, I Can Make You Feel Good, in 2020, and says he is hungry to make more.
